en: A Brief Exposition of the Method for the Seven-Limb Recitation and Practice according to the *Mahāvairocana-buddhābhisambodhi-vikurvāṇa-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*.
By [the one holding the rank of] Kai-fu Yi-tong-san-si, Te-jin, Shi Hong-lu-qing, and Duke of Su.
I prostrate to the one of unimpeded wisdom, the son born from the intention of the Secret Teaching;
relying upon that sūtra, I shall here summarize the methods for its practice.
For the bodhisattva of mantra practice, there is the vow of non-abiding and peerlessness.
The secret of speech together with the secret of body, followed by the practice of union.
The samaya mantra is as follows:
"The mudrā consists of aligning all the wheels, and joining them secretly to establish the two voids."
At the five locations— the crown, shoulders, and heart— finally adding the position of the throat; next,
one binds the mudrā of the Arising of the Dharmadhātu, the emblem of secret wisdom,
which purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind, revolving throughout the entire body.
The mantra for the Arising of the Dharmadhātu is as follows:
With the hands of Prajñā and Samādhi, both form vajra-fists;
pressing them together, erect the wind-banner; keeping them straight, cause them to join.
This is called the Dharma-realm, the pure secret seal.
Just as the self-nature of the Dharma-realm, one contemplates one's own body as stainless and equal to space through the power of the mantra and the seal.
Next, one binds the Wheel of Dharma mudrā;
this supreme empowerment causes that [being] to attain firmness.
The hands of śamatha and vipaśyanā are turned back-to-back, with the wheels of earth, water, fire, and wind.
Holding the left and right hands together, rotate both palms in the two voids;
joining them within the palm of wisdom is called the "Supreme Dharma Wheel.
The mantra of Vajrasattva is as follows:
While reciting this secret mantra, one should abide in meditative equipoise (samādhi) and clearly visualize one’s own form as Vajradhara.
All the great māras and those who behold him directly—
Like Vajrasattva, do not give rise to a doubting mind.
Next, with the Noble Acala, dispel obstacles and remove defilements;
thus one can purify all matters, performing the binding and protection according to the appropriate rites.
The mantra of Acala is as follows:
Place the syllables for earth and water upon the foundation of space and concentration; Place wind and fire vertically at the heart.
The sword of wisdom is likewise; Drawn from its scabbard, it can accomplish all tasks.
Next, with the Tathāgata Hook, invite the Honored One and the assembly of noble ones;
through the application of secret skillful means, they descend in accordance with their original vows.
The mantra of the Tathāgata Hook is as follows:
The internal aspects of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are intertwined; the wisdom-wind is held upright.
Just slightly bending the first finger, the remaining fingers form a ring-like shape.
By the power of the Noble One’s compassionate vow, he descends in response to every invocation.
Present the samaya offerings; the mantras and mudrās are as previously described.
Having manifested one’s original vow, one will certainly attain union.
Next, according to one's capacity, perform offerings to express a sincere heart.
With argha, incense, food, and lamps— down to even a single flower or a drop of water—
or by merely exercising the power of visualization and thought, the merit is supreme and most immeasurable.
One should employ the ordinary mudrā, along with the meditative practice and the mantra.
Both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) are fully accomplished.
The Universal Mantra is as follows:
Join the hands of Samādhi and Prajñā together, with the right hand interlaced above at the first joints.
With a mind that pervades everywhere, whatever is contemplated appears before one.
Having thus performed the offerings, one should cultivate the constant practice of recitation;
first donning the vajra armor, one performs the rites of protection in accordance with the ritual procedures.
The mantra of the Vajra Armor is as follows:
First, join the palms with hollowed centers; interlace the wind-wheels (the ring fingers) while supporting the fire-wheels (the middle fingers);
let the great space-wheels (the thumbs) rest upon the base of the fire-wheels; and finally, touch all parts while placing [the thumbs] at the heart.
Next, bind the boundaries of the cardinal and intermediate directions:
using the previously mentioned Acala, turn to the left to perform the expulsion;
turning to the right, as well as upward and downward, touch all parts of the body. Thus binding the protection, it becomes entirely firm and secure.
The mudrā of the Mother of True Speech has already been analyzed as before.
Once it has been fully prepared, one should display the fundamental seal (*mūla-mudrā*),
applying it again to the five locations seven times or twice over.
Forming the mudrā, open it above the crown of the head;
with the body in half-lotus posture and the mind composed, or assuming the appropriate cross-legged seat according to the directions taught.
Standing before the main image, gaze upon a single, luminous, circular form.
Pure and free from blemish, like the full orb of the moon,
within which is the form of the Principal Deity; its wondrous color transcends the three realms,
its body adorned with garments of fine gauze, a jeweled crown upon its head with dark blue hair flowing down.
In the samādhi of profound stillness, its radiant blaze surpasses all lightning;
like within a pure mirror, the subtle and deep reveals the true countenance.
Joy and anger manifest as forms and colors; their maintenance and aspirations are equal.
With a body in meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*), the mind is clear and undisturbed;
possessing the essence of the signless pure Dharma, one responds to vows to deliver all sentient beings.
With focused concentration, one maintains mindfulness and recitation; once the allotted number of repetitions is completed, [the practice is finished].
Only after one's exhaustion has reached its limit does one rest.
With sincere devotion, one should make aspirations and the like, and with earnest gravity, pay homage to the Holy Lord.
Turning to the left without force, one releases the previously established protection.
Returning, present the mudrā of the Honored One and open it above the crown of the head.
Direct the mind toward the Holy Deity, prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground, and then rise to follow the assembly in virtuous conduct; at the subsequent gathering, proceed as before.
Sometimes with two or three, or four—all likewise;
others circumambulate the stūpa, bathe the image, and recite the Mahāyāna.
They adorn the maṇḍala, scatter flowers, and praise the Buddha’s virtues.
Alternatively, being free from discursive thoughts, one focuses single-mindedly on meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).
By thus purifying the three doors of action, *siddhi* will swiftly manifest before one;
for, through the empowerment of the Noble Ones, one’s conduct and aspirations are brought into harmony.
All those who delight in cultivation, Who receive and learn from their teachers,
And uphold the mantras and the original teachings, Do not transgress the samaya.
Exerting themselves in uninterrupted practice, They remain free from hindrances and the intoxication of defilements.
By practicing the various precepts in accordance with the teachings, Siddhi will be accomplished according to one's capacity.
Relying upon the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, I briefly demonstrate the practice of yoga;
May the cultivation and realization of this sublime merit Universally moisten and benefit all sentient beings.
A Single Fascicle of the Ritual Manual for the Seven-Limb Recitation as Briefly Illustrated in the Mahāvairocana Sūtra.
